doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Teaching swing and Butterfly Lovers in Beijing 1997
summary: How swing is learned, Murray's soul-jazz take on Butterfly Lovers, and Beijing audiences rejecting Chinese instruments in jazz in 1997.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: That defining swing is always a hard thing to do. Are there words that you can use? Or is it more of a trying to show them with your instrument?

It’s like anything, you have to work with it and you have to work with people that do it, and you have to do it on a consistent level. Because nobody can just say — somebody who’s in this tradition suddenly you can do that. And I think David Murray respects that. You can’t make him play a Chinese melody like a Chinese person. But what I did do was take the Chinese melody and let him hear, by the Chinese musicians, but then play it the way he does, which is, on the “Butterfly Lover” song he treats it almost like a Cannonball Adderley fifties funk, that Gospel funk.

And so he tears it up. And the Chinese musicians love it. Now that’s the Chinese musicians in the United States, and possibly the young Chinese musicians. But if you brought it over to China, which we did, in Beijing, the Beijing International Jazz Festival in 1997, they’re so used to hearing the “Butterfly Lover” song the way it’s performed by the classical orchestra, violin concerto, that was composed by Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai in 1958, that they just can’t accept it. In fact they don’t even want to see Chinese instruments in jazz. They want to see authentic jazz, see. And so right now in this time, 2003, they’re not ready for what I’m offering.
